Karlovac Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Karlovac, Croatia

Not demolished. Karlovac, founded in 1579 as an anti-Ottoman fortress and named for Archduke Karl II of Austria, resisted seven Turkish siege attempts, the last in 1672; by the 18th century it became a major regional trading hub for wheat, corn, salt, timber, and tobacco, further boosted by an 1861 railway connection. Jews first arrived in the late 18th century (41 by 1785); the formal community organized in 1852 with 130 members, later joined by Jewish families from Slovakia and Bohemia. Most Jews lived in the 'Zidovska Város' quarter near the old Dubovak fortress - not a segregated ghetto, as Christian families lived there too - working prominently in business, banking, and international trade. Population reached 905 by 1880; a grand 1871 Neolog synagogue, with an organ and Jerusalem-facing façade, was among Croatia's most beautiful. Postwar economic decline reduced the community to 198 by 1940, with about half its members intermarried with non-Jews before WWII. During the Holocaust, 86% of local Jews perished in concentration camps; the synagogue became a warehouse, ultimately ruined in 1961, leaving just 25 Jews in Karlovac by 1971. This cemetery, established near the old Dubovak fortress at the start of the 19th century (oldest tombstone 1816), gained its own burial society in 1825, which built a newer cemetery here in 1891 featuring marble gravestones and an antique-temple-styled mortuary. The site was nationalized in 1958 and protected as a historical landmark, though 1988 vandalism by right-wing extremists painted swastikas and damaged tombstones.
